A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RELGT research. Their complete main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and matchable despite layout changes and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix A report original RELGT benchmark results, component and context-size ablations, positional-encoding experiments and runtime measurements.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional spatio-temporal encoding experiments and Griffin comparisons in Appendix A.3–A.4.

M1.justification: The main five-component RELGT architecture is unchanged. Appendix A.3 adds an experimental alternative that initializes the subgraph GNN with relative time and replaces the separate temporal and structural encoders with one joint encoder, producing a four-component token representation.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 21 classification and regression tasks across seven RelBench datasets. The new encoding and Griffin experiments use subsets of this existing coverage; recommendation tasks remain excluded.

E2.justification: Appendix A.4 and Table 6 add Griffin as a comparator on ten existing classification tasks. The original HeteroGNN, HGT and HGT+PE comparator set is retained in the main experiments.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce an eight-task joint-encoder control and task-specific Griffin fine-tuning on ten classification tasks. Section 4.2 also introduces a ±1% relative-performance rule for calling results comparable. Existing splits, MAE/AUC metrics and stated training settings remain unchanged; the revised HGT scores are not accompanied by a reported setting change.

E4.justification: New Appendix A.3 and Table 5 test whether joint spatio-temporal encoding can replace separate temporal and structural encoders, reporting worse test performance on all eight tested tasks. Existing component-removal, context-size, depth/dropout and random-versus-Laplacian initialization studies are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 11–12 add ± values throughout the test and validation results for all four methods across 21 tasks; the corresponding v1 Tables 9–10 contain only point estimates. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting, although v2 does not define the ± statistic or provide run counts or seeds, so additional replication cannot be established.

E6.justification: HGT and HGT+PE test scores change on 19 of 21 tasks each, while RDL and RELGT point estimates remain unchanged. For example, HGT study-adverse MAE changes from 43.3253 to 45.1692, reversing its ranking against RDL at 44.473. New Tables 5–6 report losses for joint encoding on eight tasks and RELGT wins over Griffin on eight of ten tasks.

T1.justification: Appendix A.7 adds per-node attention complexity statements of O(K²d) locally and O(KBd) globally. Appendix A.3 also formally defines the joint encoding in Equations 11–12. Original mathematical definitions and Equations 1–10 remain unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: the first graph transformer specifically designed for relational entity graphs, five-element tokenization, combined local/global attention, and improvements of up to 18% across the same 21-task evaluation.

C2.justification: Section 4.2 qualifies the performance discussion using the new ±1% rule: ten improvements, nine comparable outcomes and two losses. Appendix A.4 interprets the Griffin comparison as supporting a transformer backbone. Existing explanations of task-dependent global context, encoding redundancy and temporal noise remain.

D1.justification: Existing implementation and reproducibility disclosures are retained: learning rate, layer/dropout search, context and centroid sizes, batch sizes, HGT implementation details, PyTorch/PyG software, A100 hardware and code-access information. No separate new implementation settings or access resources accompany the added experiments.

R1.justification: New Section 2.4 explicitly distinguishes RELGT from HTGformer and existing subgraph transformers, while Appendix A.4 positions it against Griffin. References add HTGformer and Griffin and remove Kim et al.'s Pure Transformers Are Powerful Graph Learners. The overall research positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are preserved. Changes include localized wording edits, author–year citations, conference headers, the new addressing-challenges subsection, two additional appendix subsections and corrected cross-references.

P2.justification: The revision adds Tables 5–6, resizes and reflows existing tables, accommodates ± entries in the detailed result tables, and adopts ICLR typography and headers. Figures 1–5 retain their visual content, with changes to sizing or placement.

improvement.justification: The Griffin comparison and joint-encoding ablation add useful evidence about competitiveness and design choices, while the ±1% discussion clarifies wins, near-ties and losses. These are limited gains: uncertainty statistics and run counts remain undefined, and revised HGT scores are not reconciled with Table 7 or the discussion. For example, Section 4.2 says PE helps on eight tasks, whereas the revised Table 1 shows twelve.
